title: Significance level
keyIdea: The significance level α is the threshold probability for rejecting the null hypothesis, often 5% or 1%, and it is fixed before the data are collected. If H₀ is true, the chance of wrongly rejecting it (a Type I error) is at most α. The critical region is the set of most extreme results whose total probability under H₀ is at or below α; for X ~ B(20, 0.5) with H₁: p > 0.5 at 5% it is X ≥ 15, and because X is discrete the actual significance level is P(X ≥ 15) ≈ 2.07%. A smaller α, such as 1%, means fewer false rejections but makes a real effect harder to detect. Not rejecting H₀ is not proof that H₀ is true.
familyTip: Ask your teenager: if a friend claims a coin is biased, how many heads out of 20 would it take before they believed it? Then ask whether they would want the bar set at 5% or at 1%, and what each choice risks.

visual.caption: X ~ B(20, 0.5), H₁: p > 0.5, α = 5%, critical region X ≥ 15. Reject H₀? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: fix α before the data, find critical regions for 10%, 5% and 1%, simulate Type I errors, compare 5% with 1% on a biased coin, and decide.

kid: A test needs a rule for when to reject H₀. The rule is the significance level, called α. It is a probability, often 5% or 1%. You choose it before you see any data. If you chose it after, the result could tempt you to move the line.
Say H₀ is true, but you reject it anyway. That is a Type I error. With α = 5%, this happens in at most 5% of tests. Run many tests on a fair coin and only a few reject H₀.

The critical region is the set of results that make you reject H₀. Take X ~ B(20, 0.5) and H₁: p > 0.5. P(X ≥ 15) is about 2.07%, but P(X ≥ 14) is about 5.77%. So at 5% the region is X ≥ 15. Its true size, 2.07%, is the actual significance level.

A smaller α, like 1%, needs stronger evidence. Fewer true H₀s are thrown out. But a real bias is missed more often. If you do not reject H₀, you have not proved it. There is just not enough evidence against it.
adult: Ages 16 to 18. This is A level Mathematics statistics. Students must know the words of a hypothesis test: significance level, critical value, critical region, acceptance region and p-value. They carry out one-tailed and two-tailed binomial tests. The significance level α is a threshold set in advance. The actual significance level is the probability of the critical region if H₀ is true. For a discrete variable it is usually less than α.

The trade-off. α is the maximum probability of a Type I error, rejecting H₀ when it is true. Lowering α shrinks the critical region, so the test makes fewer false rejections but more Type II errors, failing to reject a false H₀. In the lab, with p really 0.7 and n = 20, the test rejects about 42% of the time at 5% (X ≥ 15) but only about 24% at 1% (X ≥ 16). Choosing α after seeing the data, or changing it to get a result, invalidates the test.

Common mistakes. Students read 5% as the chance that H₀ is true. They include a value whose tail is just over α, such as X ≥ 14 with a tail of 5.77%. They quote α when asked for the actual level, or compare the p-value with the wrong level. They write 'accept H₀' or 'H₀ is true'. The right wording is 'there is not enough evidence to reject H₀', followed by a conclusion in context.

practice.prompt: What does a 5% significance level mean?
choices: If H₀ is true, there is at most a 5% chance of rejecting it
There is a 5% chance that H₀ is true
The data are 95% accurate
practice.hint: α is a probability worked out assuming H₀ is true. What event is it the probability of?
practice.explain: α is the largest probability you accept of rejecting H₀ when H₀ is actually true, a Type I error. It is not the probability that H₀ is true.

practice.prompt: A test at α = 5% is run {=n*100} times, and H₀ is true every time. At most about how many times would you expect H₀ to be rejected?
practice.hint: If H₀ is true, each test rejects with probability at most 0.05.
practice.explain: 0.05 × {=n*100} = {=n*5}. Each of those rejections would be a Type I error.

practice.prompt: A test at α = 1% is run {=n*100} times, and H₀ is true every time. At most about how many false rejections would you expect?
practice.hint: 1% of the tests, at most. What is 1% of {=n*100}?
practice.explain: 0.01 × {=n*100} = {n}. A smaller α means fewer Type I errors.

practice.prompt: X ~ B(20, 0.5) under H₀, H₁: p > 0.5. P(X ≥ 14) = 5.77% and P(X ≥ 15) = 2.07%. What is the critical region at the 5% level?
practice.hint: Find the biggest upper tail whose probability is at or below 5%.
practice.explain: P(X ≥ 14) = 5.77% is over 5%, so 14 is not included. P(X ≥ 15) = 2.07% fits, so the critical region is X ≥ 15.

practice.prompt: Why must the significance level be chosen before the data are collected?
choices: So the result cannot sway where the line is drawn
Because the data cannot be collected without it
So that the test is sure to reject H₀
practice.hint: What could happen if you saw a p-value of 3% and then had to pick α?
practice.explain: If α were chosen after seeing the data, you could pick a level that gives the answer you want. Fixing it first keeps the Type I error rate at α.

pool.prompt: The p-value is 3% and the test is at the 1% level. What should you conclude?
choices: Do not reject H₀: there is not enough evidence at the 1% level
Reject H₀, because 3% is small
H₀ is proved true
pool.hint: Compare the p-value with α. Is 3% below 1%?
pool.explain: 3% is not below 1%, so the result is not significant at the 1% level. Do not reject H₀, but this does not prove H₀ true.

pool.prompt: A scientist switches a test from 5% to 1%. What is the effect?
choices: Fewer false rejections, but a real effect is harder to detect
The test becomes more accurate in every way
H₀ becomes easier to reject
pool.hint: A smaller α needs a more extreme result before you reject H₀.
pool.explain: A 1% level cuts the chance of a Type I error, but the critical region shrinks, so a real effect is missed more often (more Type II errors).

pool.prompt: For X ~ B(20, 0.5), the 5% critical region is X ≥ 15. What is the actual significance level?
choices: Exactly 5%
pool.hint: The actual level is the probability of landing in the critical region if H₀ is true.
pool.explain: X is discrete, so the tail cannot hit 5% exactly. The actual significance level is P(X ≥ 15) ≈ 2.07%.

pool.prompt: What is a Type I error?
choices: Rejecting H₀ when H₀ is actually true
Not rejecting H₀ when H₀ is false
Using the wrong distribution for X
pool.hint: Which mistake does the significance level control?
pool.explain: A Type I error is rejecting a true H₀. Its probability is at most α. Missing a false H₀ is a Type II error.

pool.prompt: {=n*20} schools each run a fair test at the 5% level, and H₀ is true at every school. At most about how many schools would wrongly reject H₀?
pool.hint: Each test has at most a 5% chance of a Type I error. What is 5% of {=n*20}?
pool.explain: 0.05 × {=n*20} = {n}. Those schools would reject a true H₀ just by chance.

pool.prompt: A medical trial is run at the 1% level at {=n*100} hospitals, and the drug has no effect (H₀ is true) at every hospital. At most about how many hospitals would wrongly conclude that the drug works?
pool.hint: Each hospital has at most a 1% chance of a Type I error. What is 1% of {=n*100}?
pool.explain: 0.01 × {=n*100} = {n}. Those hospitals would reject a true H₀ just by chance.

pool.prompt: X ~ B(20, 0.5), H₁: p > 0.5, α = 5%. You observe 14 heads. Conclusion?
choices: Do not reject H₀: P(X ≥ 14) = 5.77% is over 5%
Reject H₀: 14 is well above 10
Reject H₀: 14 is in the critical region
pool.hint: Is 14 in the critical region X ≥ 15?
pool.explain: 14 is outside the critical region X ≥ 15, and P(X ≥ 14) = 5.77% is more than 5%. There is not enough evidence to reject H₀.

pool.prompt: Sam sees a p-value of 4%, then decides to use a 5% level so the result counts. What is wrong?
choices: α must be fixed before the data, not chosen to fit the result
Nothing, 4% is below 5%
The p-value should have been 5% exactly
pool.hint: When should the significance level be set?
pool.explain: Picking α after seeing the p-value lets the data choose the rule, so the real Type I error rate is no longer α.

pool.prompt: X ~ B(20, 0.5), H₁: p > 0.5. P(X ≥ 16) = 0.59% and P(X ≥ 15) = 2.07%. What is the critical region at the 1% level?
pool.hint: Find the biggest upper tail with probability at or below 1%.
pool.explain: P(X ≥ 15) = 2.07% is over 1%. P(X ≥ 16) = 0.59% fits, so the 1% critical region is X ≥ 16.
